fixes.explanation: That's it. The king plans to set Daniel over the whole kingdom. That's every satrap, every administrator and everybody else. I can barely supervise one batch, and the king plans to hand Daniel the entire operation.

An army is a big job, but the text doesn't say that. It says the king planned to set Daniel over the whole kingdom. An ARMY? That's the starter package, baker. Daniel's extraordinary spirit has really made him stand out.
That's the reason the text gives. Verse 4 says they found no charge “…because he was trustworthy…” and no negligence or corruption was found in him. That's a hard record to dig through.
His family back in Judah? Nobody brings them up, friend. The men say they need something “…concerning the law of his God.” That's the one target they name. They are going after how he serves God.

Hiding would be a sensible plan, but that's not what the text says. Daniel prays in his upper room where the windows open toward Jerusalem. He prays three times a day, “…just as he had done before.” He kept to his usual routine instead of switching to secret prayers.

Yes, his upper room windows open toward Jerusalem. The text says that's where he kneels, prays and gives thanks. Daniel was one of the exiles from Judah (Daniel 6:13), so I think that direction means something to him. That's my guess, though, not the text's.
Persia comes up in the chapter, but not in this verse. The windows of his upper room open toward Jerusalem. That's the room where he kneels and prays.

Egypt? Friend, that's not even on the map for this story. Daniel's upper room has windows that open toward Jerusalem. That's where he gets down on his knees, prays and gives thanks to his God three times a day.

That's the opposite of what the text says. Verse 14 tells us the king was deeply distressed and set his mind on delivering Daniel. A man who's relieved doesn't labor until sundown trying to rescue someone.
The king isn't laughing in this verse, friend. The text says Darius was deeply distressed and set his mind on delivering Daniel. A man who's amused doesn't labor until sundown to rescue someone.
Yes. The text says the king set his mind on delivering Daniel and labored until sundown to rescue him. That's real effort from a king. Darius isn't just sitting on the throne watching.
It's true, baker. Verse 14 says the king set his mind on delivering Daniel, and he labored until sundown to rescue him. The decree was signed, so it didn't get him anywhere, but he tried.

That's the word. The king seals the stone with his own signet ring and the rings of his nobles, “…so that nothing concerning Daniel could be changed.” It's a lot of rings for one stone. Those rings were there to keep everything exactly as it was.
Daniel doesn't say a prophet. He says, “My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions.” The one God sent is an angel, and the result is that the lions' mouths are shut.
That's the reason Daniel gives. He says, “…for I was found innocent in His sight…” He adds that he has done no wrong against the king, too.
The fasting that night is the king's (Daniel 6:18). Daniel's own reason is, “…for I was found innocent in His sight…” That's the reason he gives for why the lions haven't hurt him.

Darius says the opposite. About Daniel's God, the king writes, “…He endures forever; His kingdom will never be destroyed, and His dominion will never end.” That's a king declaring that God's kingdom has no end. He had just seen Daniel rescued from the lions.
